23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *ALDH5A1* variant or a diagnosis of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.

29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.

36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *ALDH5A1* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.

42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:

45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.

52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.

57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.

96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.

105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *ALDH5A1* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");

167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:

170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

2	
3	1. Use only the supplied document. Do not use outside knowledge about the gene, the disease, specific variants or specific patients. If the document does not state something, the value is "not reported" (for text fields) or null (for numeric and date fields). Never fill a gap from memory.
4	2. Every value must be supported by a verbatim quote copied exactly from the document. Do not paraphrase inside the quote. If no exact quote supports a value, do not emit the value.
5	3. Keep original strings. Record variant descriptions, ages, feature names and labels exactly as printed. Never convert protein-only variant descriptions into cDNA notation, never add a transcript that is not printed, never translate units.
6	4. Three-state phenotypes: a feature is "observed" only when the document says the person has or had it, and "excluded" only when the document explicitly says it was absent, negative or not found in that person. Silence is "not reported". Never turn silence into "excluded".
7	5. One row per real person per document. Relatives described in the document are their own rows with is_proband = false unless the document calls them probands. Do not merge people, and do not create a person the document does not describe.
8	6. Cohort tables: when a table lists many patients, extract each patient row separately with the table's own patient identifier as individual_label_in_paper. Keep the row-to-column alignment of the table; when a cell is empty or marked "-", "NA" or "ND", treat it as not reported.
9	7. Re-reports: if the document says that any of its patients were described in an earlier publication, record that statement and the citation in the publications table. Do not drop the patient.
10	8. Do not infer inheritance or zygosity. "de novo" requires that the document states parental testing showed the variant absent in both parents. "heterozygous" requires that the document says so or the gene is described as monoallelic for that person.
11	9. Prefer "not reported" to a plausible guess. Abstention is correct behaviour.

7	
8	# Metabolic Stroke: A Novel Presentation in a Child with Succinic Semialdehyde Dehydrogenase Deficiency
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder of gamma-aminobutyric acid metabolism. Children with SSADH deficiency usually manifest with developmental delay, behavioral symptoms, language dysfunction, seizures, hypotonia, extrapyramidal symptoms, and ataxia. Diagnosis of SSADH deficiency is established by an abnormal urine organic acid pattern, including increased excretion of 4-hydroxybutyric acid and the identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in aldehyde dehydrogenase 5 family, member A 1 (ALDH5A1) gene. Here, we describe a 15-month-old girl with SSADH deficiency presenting with developmental delay, language deficits, and acute-onset right hemiparesis, following recovery from a diarrheal illness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed hyperintense signal changes involving the left globus pallidus in T2-weighted images with restriction of diffusion in the diffusion-weighted images. Increased excretion of 4-hydroxybutyric acid, threo-4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acid lactone and erythro-4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acid lactone was detected by urine organic acid analysis and a diagnosis of SSADH deficiency was confirmed by the identification of homozygous pathogenic variant in ALDH5A1. Stroke mimic is a novel presentation in our patient with SSADH deficiency. She was initiated on treatment with vigabatrin and has shown developmental gains with the recovery of right hemiparesis. Follow-up neuroimaging shows near complete resolution of signal changes in the left globus pallidus, while there was subtle hyperintensity in the right globus pallidus. The phenotypic spectrum of SSADH deficiency is widely expanding, and this disorder should be considered in the differential diagnosis of children with metabolic stroke.
13	
14	## INTRODUCTION
15	
16	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) metabolism manifesting with developmental delay, language deficits, behavioral symptoms, hypotonia, extrapyramidal symptoms, ataxia, and epilepsy.[1] Diagnosis of SSADH deficiency is established by the identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in aldehyde dehydrogenase 5 family, member A1 (ALDH5A1) gene. SSADH deficiency shows both intrafamilial and interfamilial phenotypic heterogeneity with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations and wide age range of presentations.[1] Here, we describe a 15-month-old girl with biochemical and molecular confirmation of SSADH deficiency presenting with acute-onset right hemiparesis, following recovery from a diarrheal illness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hyperintense signal changes involving the left globus pallidus. To the best of our knowledge, stroke mimic is a novel presentation in patients with SSADH deficiency.
17	
18	## CASE REPORT
19	
20	A 15-month-old girl, second born to third-degree consanguineously married parents from India, without apparent antenatal or neonatal risk factors, presented with a history of acute-onset paucity of movements in the right upper and lower limbs. At the onset, she had multiple episodes of yellowish, watery stools mixed with mucus for 3 days. There was no history of vomiting or decreased urine output. On the 3^rd day of illness, she had high-grade fever which was not associated with cough, cold, or ear discharge. The fever had subsided on the 4^th day. She had sustained a trivial fall while playing on the 8^th day and hit her head against the wall. There was no history of vomiting, bleeding, seizures, or loss of consciousness. Two days later, parents observed an acute-onset paucity of movements of the right upper and lower limbs. There was no history of vision or hearing disturbances, deviation of angle of the mouth, drooping of the eyelids, swallowing dysfunction, nasal twang, or nasal regurgitation. There was history of recurrent episodes of fast breathing in the past, and she was treated elsewhere with nebulization and oral antibiotics.
21	
22	Premorbidly, the child could walk few steps with support, hold objects by pincer grasp, and she had stranger anxiety. She could not wave bye–bye, and there was no reciprocative babbling. There was only a poor response to name call, but her vision was normal. Apart from her mother, who had paralytic poliomyelitis in the childhood, her family history was noncontributory.
23	
24	Anthropometry assessment at the time of presentation revealed a head circumference of 44.7 cm (3^rd to 50^th centile), weight of 10 kg (50^th to 97^th centile), and length of 80 cm (50^th to 97^th centile). Fleeting eye contact and fidgetiness were observed. She did not obey single-step commands and did not communicate her needs. She was not interested in her surroundings and displayed poor social interaction. Cranial nerve examination was normal. Tone was decreased in the right more than the left upper and lower limbs. Antigravity movements were preserved in the left side, while on the right side, she had only gravity eliminated movements. Deep tendon reflexes were diminished bilaterally. Bilateral plantar responses were extensor.
25	
26	Initial possibilities considered were basal ganglia stroke following trivial trauma, demyelinating illness, or an organic aciduria such as methylmalonic acidemia or propionic acidemia. Stool enzyme-linked immunoassay was negative for rotavirus. Blood sugar and serum electrolytes were normal. Computerized tomography of the brain done in the acute phase [Figure 1a] showed hypodensity involving the left globus pallidus. MRI of the brain in the acute phase [Figure 1b-d] had revealed hyperintensity of the left globus pallidus on the T2-weighted axial image with restriction of diffusion in the left globus pallidus on the diffusion-weighted images. Electroencephalography (EEG) was normal. Visual evoked potential and brainstem auditory evoked responses were normal. Somatosensory-evoked potential of the tibial nerves had shown bilateral peripheral pathway dysfunction. Serum amino acid profile performed by high-performance liquid chromatography and acylcarnitine analyses performed by tandem mass spectrometry were normal. However, urine organic acid analysis performed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GCMS) revealed increased excretion of 4-hydroxybutyric acid and threo- and erythro-4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acid lactones, consistent with a diagnosis of SSADH deficiency (OMIM ID-#271980). This diagnosis was confirmed by the mutation analysis of ALDH5A1. Sanger sequencing of ALDH5A1 revealed a homozygous variant, c.1343 + 1_1343 + 3delGTAinsTT, leading to a change in the consensus splice donor site of exon 8/intron 8 (Transcript ID ENST00000357578 with genomic coordinate Chr6: 24528395_24528397 delGTAinsTT; GRCh 37/hg19 build). Her parents were heterozygous for the same variant [Figure 2]. This variant is predicted to be pathogenic by various in silico prediction analysis tools and is previously reported as pathogenic in ClinVar database with submission accession SCV000268064.1 and allele ID-227703 (The Single-Nucleotide Polymorphism Database [dbSNP] ID-875989801).
27	
28	**Figure 1**: (a) Computed tomography brain showing hypodensity of the left globus pallidus (white arrow). (b) Magnetic resonance imaging brain: T2-weighted axial images showing hyperintensity of the left globus pallidus (white arrow). (c) Diffusion-weighted images showing hyperintensity in the left globus pallidus (black arrow) and (d) apparent diffusion coefficient images show low signal in the left globus pallidus (black arrow)
29	
30	**Figure 2**: Electropherogram showing homozygous pathogenic variant, c.1343 + 1_1343 + 3delGTAinsTT, leading to a change in the consensus splice donor site of exon 8/intron 8 in proband. Parents and the unaffected sibling are heterozygous for the same variant
31	
32	Once the diagnosis of SSADH deficiency was confirmed, treatment with vigabatrin in addition to the standard supportive measures was initiated. Follow-up assessment after 6 months revealed mild developmental gains. Hypotonia persisted, but the right hemiparesis had resolved. Follow-up imaging [Figure 3a-c] showed a near complete resolution of signal changes in the left globus pallidus and a subtle hyperintensity in the right globus pallidus on the T2-weighted axial image while the diffusion-weighted images were normal. Significant developmental gains were observed during a follow-up assessment after 2 years from the time of diagnosis.
33	
34	**Figure 3**: (a) Magnetic resonance imaging brain: T2-weighted axial image at follow-up showing near complete resolution of signal changes in the left globus pallidus, while a subtle hyperintensity is seen in the right globus pallidus (white arrow). (b and c) Diffusion-weighted images and apparent diffusion coefficient images at follow-up are normal
35	
36	## DISCUSSION
37	
38	SSADH deficiency is a rare under-recognized disorder of GABA metabolism, although the exact incidence is not known. In our case, developmental delay, language deficit, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, and autistic traits were identified as described in the literature. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of a child with SSADH deficiency presenting as stroke mimic. The biochemical defect in SSADH deficiency is a failure to oxidize succinic semialdehyde to succinic acid. GABA transamination to succinic semialdehyde in the metabolic pathway is followed by its conversion to succinic acid which enters the Krebs cycle.[2] However, in the absence of SSADH, succinic semialdehyde is reduced to 4-hydroxybutyric acid which is a neurotoxic agent.[2] Predominant right-sided weakness in our case could be explained by the asymmetric involvement of the basal ganglia.
39	
40	Metabolic stroke has been reported in patients with homocystinuria, methylmalonic aciduria, glutaric aciduria Type I and II, isovaleric aciduria, propionic aciduria, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), Fabry disease, and urea cycle disorders.[34] The exact pathophysiology of stroke in patients with SSADH is unclear. It is possible that 4-hydroxybutyric acid, a toxic metabolite that accumulates endogenously in children with SSADH deficiency, is neurotoxic as seen in our patient, leading onto the clinical manifestations. Although the exact reason behind such a presentation is unclear, we can derive at an indirect explanation through the murine models of SSADH. It is postulated that hyperGABAergic state and elevated 4-hydroxybutyric acid affect neurotransmission and also cause escalation of various parameters of oxidative stress.[5] The catabolic process induced by infection as seen in our case might have worsened the underlying oxidative stress, followed by recovery with the cessation of the catabolic process.
41	
42	Seizures are reported in nearly half of patients with SSADH deficiency, and various seizure semiology reported in these patients are generalized tonic–clonic seizures, absence seizures, partial and myoclonic seizures.[6] EEG abnormalities documented in patients with SSADH deficiency are background slowing, epileptiform discharges, electrical status epilepticus, asynchronous sleep spindles, and photosensitivity.[67] On the contrary, EEG may be normal in patients with SSADH deficiency.[6] Our patient had no seizures or electroencephalographic abnormalities. Dystonia, ataxia, and sleep disturbances were also absent in our patient. Although hyporeflexia was documented in our case, nerve conduction parameters were normal for age.
43	
44	Psychiatric symptoms described in patients with SSADH deficiency include sleep disorders, anxiety, pervasive developmental disorder, obsessive–compulsive disorder, hallucinations, aggression, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.[8] Similarly, features of fleeting eye contact, fidgetiness, and lack of social interaction were observed in our case. Ocular manifestations such as strabismus, retinitis, nystagmus, and oculomotor apraxia have been described in patients with SSADH deficiency.[9] In contrast, no ocular manifestations were detected in our patient.
45	
46	Blood tandem mass spectrometry was normal in our case, while urine GCMS had revealed increased excretion of 4-hydroxybutyric acid and threo- and erythro-4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acid lactones, consistent with the diagnosis of SSADH deficiency. Our case emphasizes the importance and utility of urine GCMS in the diagnosis of metabolic disorders. The pathogenic variant detected in our case has likely been identified in at least three additional families, although the authors have used different nomenclature on at least two occasions. One author in the previous report used a mutation nomenclature with variants in two different nucleotide positions interspersed by a single wild-type allele (The two variants were c.1343 + 1delG and c.1343 + 3A>T with IDs in human gene mutation database: CD33523 and CS33487, respectively). It is unlikely that two variants coexisting independently with a wild type allele interspersed without any clear evidence of support.[10] It is our opinion that an “indel” is more plausible than two independent mutational events occurring de novo with blurring of the consequences of each event. The above-mentioned variant has been reported in ClinVar by a group from Persia with submission accession SCV000268064.1 and allele ID-227703 (dbSNP ID-rs875989801) with the indel nomenclature. Table 1 shows a comparison of the phenotype of our case and the two cases reported previously.

70	
71	Brain MRI findings in patients with SSADH deficiency include normal imaging, delayed myelination, cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintense signal changes involving bilateral globus pallidi, subthalamic nuclei, dentate nuclei, white matter, and brainstem involvement.[26] Although signal changes are symmetrical in patients with SSADH deficiency, asymmetrical or heterogeneous involvement does exist as seen in our patient.[11] Magnetic resonance spectroscopy may reveal elevated GABA and 4-hydroxybutyrate.[212] Therapeutic agents investigated in the management of SSADH deficiency are vigabatrin, taurine, NCS-382, SGS-742, and CGP-35348.[8] Vigabatrin may be used with an aim to reduce seizures and behavioral symptoms.[13] Magnesium valproate is also used in the management of epilepsy in patients with SSADH deficiency.[14] A pilot trial did not find a clinically significant improvement in the adaptive behaviour of patients with SSADH deficiency after treatment with taurine.[15] On treatment with vigabatrin, our patient had shown mild developmental gains at 6 months and significant developmental gains at 2 years of follow-up. Vigabatrin is an irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase, and variable clinical responses have been reported in patients with SSADH deficiency while on treatment with vigabatrin.[16]
72	
73	Indistinct onset and course, the presence of altered sensorium or confusional state with or without the presence of involuntary movements, and focal seizures are the clinical clues for the diagnosis of metabolic stroke.[1718] To summarize, metabolic stroke must be considered in children with developmental delay presenting with focal neurological deficits, coexistent seizures or altered sensorium, presence of multisystem involvement, positive family history, laboratory evidence of hypoglycaemia, dyselectrolytemia or acidosis, and involvement of highly metabolically active sites in brain or areas of involvement not confined to an arterial territory on the neuroimaging.
74	
75	## CONCLUSION
76	
77	The phenotypic spectrum in patients with SSADH is widely expanding. Metabolic stroke may be a presenting symptom in children with SSADH deficiency. Children with developmental delay and stroke-like presentation should be evaluated with urine organic acid screening to exclude this disorder.

5	  "relevance_note": "The paper reports one in-scope patient with SSADH deficiency and individual-level detail ('a 15-month-old girl with SSADH deficiency presenting with developmental delay, language deficits, and acute-onset right hemiparesis'), plus relatives described in relation to her and two previously reported probands with the same genotype.",
6	  "method_note": "Read the full Markdown (no supplementary material present) and transcribed everything by hand; no script was used. Labels: the paper's own labels for its patient and for the two literature patients are role words ('Proband in our report', 'Proband from Pakistan origin[1]', 'Proband from Palestinian-Lebanese origin[1]'), which the instructions say are not labels, so I used rule 5 ('patient') for the single patient of the case report and the table-column rule for the two literature patients ('Table 1 column 2', 'Table 1 column 3'); the column headers are named here. Relatives: the paper names 'her mother' (with paralytic poliomyelitis) and separately 'her parents' as carriers of the variant, so I recorded 'mother of patient' (sex stated) and 'parent of patient' for the second, unstated parent, rather than two generic parent labels; the unaffected sibling is 'sibling of patient'. Inheritance for the proband is recorded as 'inherited unspecified parent' although the paper states that both parents are heterozygous carriers, because no single-parent option fits a homozygous variant; the parents' and sibling's variant-identity fields are filled from the statement that they carry 'the same variant' whose description is printed once (transcript and genomic coordinates were not propagated to them). Stacked cells: Table 1 is a table with patients as columns; several cells hold several values printed on separate lines that the conversion ran together without ' / ' (for example '| Hypotonia | Yes | Normal tone at presentation Hypotonia at follow-up | Yes |' and '| Natural course | Resolution of hemiparesis Hypotonia persists Developmental gains are observed on treatment |'), so no positional assignment was made: each such value belongs to the patient of its own column, and no value was moved between columns. 'Age at presentation' in Table 1 was recorded as age at onset. Table 1 'Extrapyramidal symptoms: No' was recorded as a feature for the two people concerned but was not mapped onto the narrower checklist items (dystonia, exertional dyskinesia, hemiballismus), which are left 'not reported'; 'Reflexes: Normal' for the Pakistan-origin proband was recorded as excluding 'abnormal deep tendon reflexes'. 'Developmental delay' was recorded as a feature and 'intellectual disability' left 'not reported'; 'stranger anxiety' is listed among this child's developmental milestones and was not recorded as anxiety, and 'fidgetiness'/'fleeting eye contact' were not mapped to attention problems/ADHD. The in silico prediction ('predicted to be pathogenic by various in silico prediction analysis tools') is not a functional assay and was not recorded as functional evidence. The alternative nomenclature discussed for the same variant (c.1343 + 1delG and c.1343 + 3A>T) was not entered as separate variant rows because the authors argue it is the same 'indel' event. publications.n_patients_reported = 1 (one patient with a variant described first-hand); the two Table 1 probands are recorded as separate individuals with source_reference_in_review '[1]', and cites_prior_report_of_same_patients = true because the paper states that those two cases were reported previously. No internal contradictions were found.",
